rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

All pairs have substantial resolution margin, so halve the gradient time to reduce the time penalty. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed will reveal how the critical pairs respond to gradient steepness.

The fast gradient eliminates the time penalty but creates a critical overlap. Raising temperature while holding the gradient fixed tests whether selectivity can resolve that overlap while preserving the short run.

The high-temperature run fixes the original overlap but introduces another, so test the opposite temperature extreme at the same gradient slope. Lower temperature may separate the critical cluster while keeping the last peak early enough to avoid a time penalty.

Test just below 60 C to reopen the high-temperature overlap while retaining the improved separation of the original critical cluster. The last peak should remain comfortably within the zero-time-penalty region.

A slightly lower temperature should widen the pair that limits the 55 C run, while a steeper gradient may separate the temperature-reordered pair in the central cluster. This tests a route to full resolution without a time penalty.
